newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bradford sees lower NZ power prices in 12-14 mths.
newsitem.headline: Bradford sees lower NZ power prices in 12-14 mths.

text.p: New Zealand Energy Minister Max Bradford is forecasting lower power prices next year as government measures start to bite and competition comes into the retail market, the New Zealand Press Association reported on Monday.

Figures released by the Ministry of Commerce show power prices increased 5.6 percent above inflation in the year ended March 1996 and the watchdog Consumer Coalition on Energy is asking where the extra NZ$150 million went.
A spokesman for the coalition said deregulation of the energy market was supposed to produce efficiencies which would flow through to consumers, but that had not happened.
Bradford said on Monday deregulation had forced costs down at the generation end of the market and what was needed now was "real competition" at the retail end.

"We're in the process of taking a number of steps, the most radical of which is to look at whether we should formally require power companies to split their line and energy businesses," he said on National Radio.
"That's where the mischief can occur, where companies put up a series of barriers.
"They can, at least theoretically, hold up their prices by overvaluing their assets and by refusing to allow other companies to come in and compete in their areas."

Bradford said some companies had introduced household metering which allowed consumers to choose which company they bought their power from. That was a powerful element in getting competition into the market.

"The whole package of these measures we expect to have well on the way by the end of the year and I would expect within the next 12 to 14 months we'll see some quite major changes," he said when he was asked how much longer people would have to put up with high power costs.
Yesterday Alliance leader Jim Anderton accused the power companies of abusing their monopoly positions and "sucking the wallets of consumers dry".
He said the same thing had happened in Britain when the power market was deregulated and companies reaped huge profits.
"The response in Britain was the introduction by the new Labour government of a windfall profits tax to take back some of the unearned gains," he said.
"This revenue is being used to fund employment programmes and spending on essential social services. It is an idea that deserves close scrutiny."
